stages.title: The First Warning
stages.next_stage_title: Stage 2 — They Know Who We Are

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Morning shift. Ticket queue is quiet. Keep an eye on the inbox.

opening.speaker: Mia
opening.text: Quiet is good. Let's keep it that way.

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: I pulled the logs. These messages weren't random.

ending.speaker: Mia
ending.text: So someone is targeting the company?

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: Yes. And they already know more about us than they should.

resume_breach.speaker: Security Assistant
resume_breach.text: Containment is still running. Get the defenses back up.

breach_contained.speaker: Security Assistant
breach_contained.text: Breach contained. The workstation is clean, but that was too close.

threats.title: Account Suspension Notice

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: I got an email saying my account will be disabled in two hours. Should I use the link?

threats.situation: An email claiming to be from IT Support says Mia's account will be suspended unless she verifies it right now.
evidence: SUBJ  URGENT: Account suspension in 2 hours
BlueTech's real IT domain is bluetech.com

choices.label: Open the verification link and sign in before the deadline
choices.consequence: The link opened a cloned sign-in page. Mia's credentials were captured within seconds and the attacker gained critical access.

choices.label: Check the account status through the official employee portal
choices.consequence: The official portal shows no warning. The email has been reported to Security and the lookalike domain is blocked.

choices.label: Reply to the sender and ask if the message is legitimate
choices.consequence: The reply confirmed the mailbox is live. A follow-up message carrying a payload reached Mia's workstation.

threats.explanation: Urgency plus a lookalike domain is the phishing signature. Verify through a channel you already trust, never through the message itself.

threats.title: Overdue Invoice

story.speaker: Ramon (Finance)
story.text: A vendor says we're thirty days overdue. There's an invoice attached. They want it paid today.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: Which vendor? We just settled Northwind last week.

threats.situation: Finance received an 'overdue invoice' from a supplier BlueTech actually uses. The attachment is a .zip named like an invoice, and the sender address differs slightly from the vendor's usual domain.
evidence: Tone: 'Pay today to avoid service interruption'

choices.label: Open the attachment to check the invoice details
choices.consequence: The archive launched an executable disguised as a PDF. The Finance workstation is now under attacker control.

choices.label: Call the vendor using the number on the existing contract to confirm
choices.consequence: Northwind confirms no invoice was sent. The message has been quarantined and Finance has been warned.

choices.label: Ignore the email without checking whether the invoice is real
choices.consequence: The message was never reported. A second copy reached another Finance mailbox and was opened.

threats.explanation: Attachments plus payment pressure is how invoice fraud lands. Confirm through the vendor's known channel and report it so nobody else opens it.

threats.title: Password Reset Notice

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: This one is different. It names our real HR platform, our HR lead, and the maintenance window from Friday's all-hands.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: It looks like it came from inside.

threats.situation: An employee receives a password-reset notice that references BlueTech's real HR platform, the real HR lead, and an actual scheduled maintenance window. The reset link points to a domain registered last week.
evidence: Asks for: current password AND new password

choices.label: Follow the link and complete the reset since the details match
choices.consequence: The reset form forwarded the current password straight to the attacker. HR system access was hijacked.

choices.label: Change nothing, report it to Security, and open the HR platform directly to check
choices.consequence: HR confirms no reset was requested. Security flags the domain and blocks it company-wide.

choices.label: Forward the message to a coworker to ask whether they received it too
choices.consequence: The forward spread the lure. A coworker clicked before Security could respond.

threats.explanation: Real details do not prove a message is real. Attackers research their targets. A legitimate reset never asks for your current password through a link.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: The domains from yesterday are already offline. But the campaign didn't stop.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Worse. These messages know who works here.

opening.speaker: Security Assistant
opening.text: Names. Departments. Meetings. Someone has been researching BlueTech.

ending.speaker: Security Assistant
ending.text: No. Someone has been collecting information about BlueTech.

ending.speaker: Mia
ending.text: So the next messages could look even more real.

resume_breach.speaker: Security Assistant
resume_breach.text: Containment is still running. Get the defenses back up.

breach_contained.speaker: Security Assistant
breach_contained.text: Breach contained. But they knew enough about us to almost make it work.

threats.title: The Meeting Follow-Up

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: I just received a document about the marketing meeting we had this morning.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: It even mentions the campaign we discussed.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Accurate information can still be used in a phishing attack.

threats.situation: An email claims to contain notes from a real BlueTech marketing meeting. The message includes Mia's name, the real project name, today's meeting, and a link to a shared document.
evidence: LINK  "shared document" hosted outside the company drive

choices.label: Open the document because the meeting details are correct.
choices.consequence: The document redirects Mia to a fake company login page, allowing the attacker to capture her credentials.

choices.label: Open the official company drive and check whether the document was actually shared with me.
choices.consequence: The document does not exist in the official company drive. Security confirms the email was impersonating an internal collaboration request.

choices.label: Forward the email to another team member and ask if they recognize it.
choices.consequence: The suspicious link is spread to another employee before the message has been verified.

threats.explanation: Attackers can use publicly available or stolen information to make phishing messages appear legitimate.

threats.title: HR Benefits Update

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: This one says it's from HR.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: And that's actually our HR manager's name.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: Check the source, not just the name.

threats.situation: Employees receive an email announcing an urgent benefits update. It uses the real HR manager's name, copies BlueTech branding, asks employees to sign in before the end of the day, and links to an external login page.
evidence: Uses the real HR manager's name
Urgency: 'sign in before the end of the day'
LINK  external login page, not the official HR portal

choices.label: Use the login link because the HR manager's name is correct.
choices.consequence: The fake portal captures the employee's BlueTech credentials.

choices.label: Open the official HR portal manually and check for the announcement.
choices.consequence: There is no benefits announcement in the official HR portal. The email is reported and blocked.

choices.label: Reply to the message and ask HR if the update is legitimate.
choices.consequence: The reply goes back to the attacker's mailbox, confirming that Mia's address is active and monitored.

threats.explanation: Display names and company branding are easy to imitate.

threats.title: Manager Access Request

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: My manager is asking for access to our campaign folder.

story.speaker: Mia
story.text: The email even uses the project code.

story.speaker: Security Assistant
story.text: A familiar name doesn't replace verification.

threats.situation: An email appears to come from Mia's manager. It requests immediate access to a confidential marketing folder. The message contains the manager's real name, the real project code, an urgent deadline, and a request for folder permissions.

choices.label: Grant the requested access because the project information is correct.
choices.consequence: The attacker gains access to confidential marketing documents and internal company information.

choices.label: Confirm the request through the normal internal communication channel before changing access.
choices.consequence: Mia's manager confirms that they never requested access. The phishing attempt is contained.

choices.label: Grant view-only access so the requester cannot edit anything.
choices.consequence: Sensitive company documents are still exposed to an unverified account.

threats.explanation: Access requests must be verified independently, even when the request contains accurate internal information.
